en: He set aside as a vowed offering.
The many sorrows lodged in his heart,
Jakyp now laid them all aside.
From his great herds, many mares
He slaughtered to provide a feast.
Rich Jakyp's home
Filled with the forty Kyrgyz households.
When the forty Kyrgyz households had eaten their fill,
“Amen!” they said, spreading their hands,
And offered a blessing.
Bawling like a young goose,
The hero spoke in ringing bursts.
He spoke words fit for people to hear;
The hero Jakyp spoke,
Told the dream he had seen by night,
Told the good portent beneath its trouble:
“My people,
Last night, as I lay, I saw a dream;
In my dream I saw a wondrous thing.
My people, will a blessed night ever come,
When God delivers us from the Kalmyks,
Will there be a day we see the Kyrgyz?
My dream last night was an auspicious dream;
The good of that dream,
It is a splendid dream that will reach you.
Last night, as I dreamed in sleep,
I summered on the heights of Ala-Too.
A young barchyn,
An eagle, I caught.
When I went on a hunting expedition to fly it,
The beating of its wings was heard.
Unable to withstand its fury,
The creatures it attacked fell down.
It seemed to fly patrolling the world;
The black-eared leopard
Was like a mouse beneath it.
When I pulled off its hood,
It wreaked havoc;
Black-striped tigers and wild boars
It ripped apart this way and that.
Not a creature could turn it back;
All the winged creatures
Fell beneath it.
When I lifted it, its jesses numbered eighty-four;
Wherever that eagle struck
Was red fire.
Carrying it toward the sunrise,
I went on a hunting expedition.
Upon all the fanged creatures
I brought the Last Judgment.
Not letting a single one escape,
I had them torn apart and slaughtered.
In my eagerness, a whole tract of land
I plunged into crimson blood
And made it a ravine.
What can this mean?
Interpret this dream of mine.
Again, sleeping, I dreamed:
I was roaming on a mountain;
With no clear way to descend,
I was roaming on a cliff.
Unable to bear my distress,
As I stood in anger,
My honor was thus preserved:
In that dream I saw,
From the unseen, into my hand,
A Zulpukor sword appeared.
I seized it and rushed forward;
The black cliff blocking my path,
I charged at that black cliff.
When I swung, the cliff crumbled;
Unable to withstand my sword's fury,
The black cliff kept tumbling into fragments.
I toppled the deep-rooted mountain;
Everything I struck full on
I smashed to meal and brought down.
I hewed the stone and made a road;
The tangled forests and thickets
I shattered and laid low.
I broke the stone and made a road,
I humbled many a cliff,
I dried up the river,
Burned everything that faced me,
Set fire to the grassy land,
Made the cliff country level,
And made myself a khan.
Where I passed became empty, open, desolate;
Where I swung my sword became fire.
What can this mean?
My people, interpret my dream.
Again I lay and dreamed,
Again I saw a good thing.
As I lay on a hill and dreamed,
Encompassing all around,
My shade falling upon the world,
I had become a great tent.
One of its guy ropes was tied
Where the sun rises;
One of my supporting posts was planted
On the ridge where the sun sets.
My shade falling upon the world,
I lay there spread in splendor.
Rousing myself like a lion,
Pleading to God,
With one snatch of my right hand,
I caught the sun.
With one snatch of my left hand,
I caught the moon.
In my right hand stood the sun,
In my left hand stood the moon.
Grasping and turning the sun,
I put it in the moon's place;
Grasping and turning the moon,
I put it in the sun's place.
With the sun and moon together,
I struck sparks as with flint.
Interpret this dream of mine;
What can it mean?”
When he heard Jakyp's dream,
Swaying like a yellow gelded camel,
Leading the way through unknown places,
Speaking softly, laying his words down firmly,
Your elder Baltay began to speak.
Interpreting the dream that had been seen,
Akbaltay was a noble khan.
Accompanying Akbaltay,
There was a naked boy there.
A true saint, a seer,
Do not ask about your elder Akbaltay!
A seer when he spoke,
Akbaltay, champion of the tongue,
Had eloquence as well.
Akbaltay, champion of the faith,
Was an eshen as well.
He sharpened his plain tongue;
What did dear Baltay do?
He spoke in full flow among the people.
His speech rang out;
To those sorrowing Kyrgyz people
He began to speak with a bright face:
“Forty Kyrgyz households, poor people,
The yellow hills swept by sleet,
We shall find those ridges again.
O God, where our cords were cut, our birth-cloths washed,
We shall find that land again.
With the Creator granting refuge,
We shall find our people again!
What the Almighty has bestowed,
This dream that rich Jakyp saw,
That will undo great calamity,
Is this dream of rich Jakyp's.
To the Creator these Kyrgyz
Must offer supplication for this.
If this dream of yours is true,
To stir upheaval in the world,
From the Black Kalmyks and Manchus
To rescue us,
A lion of a boy will be granted us!
What was severed will be joined,
What was scattered will be gathered,
Your extinguished fire will blaze,
Your dead soul will live again!
You were forty Kyrgyz households,
Among the Black Kalmyks and Manchus
You were a people living.
Quickly vow your offering to Baabedin;
To the Creator himself,
First pledge a horse for sacrifice.
Extinguish all your sorrow;
My people, every calamity has been cut away!
At Khan Jakyp's dream,
I am swept away in wonder,
At this thing he has seen.
My heart is pounding;
Lads, among these Kalmyks,
You see, I live as one condemned.
Ah, alas, so many things come to my mind:
Where are the Kyrgyz, where are our people?
Jakyp, you have seen a wondrous dream;
Where is the day we reach our people?
Young Jakyp, my hero,
What you had in mind has been accepted!
Let me interpret the dream you saw.
Rich Jakyp, my child, take heed;
May God turn your dream to good!
My child, your climbing the mountain
Means over the seething Black Kalmyks
You have risen to the top.
If you flew a young barchyn bird
And slew the fanged beasts,
My child, you will rule the world.
Does not your barchyn mean a child?
Damn your father's grave, rich Jakyp,
You are going to have a child!
Stop your grieving, my child;
Slaughter ninety for your feast, my child.
If you flew a black barchyn bird,
Rich Jakyp, you are going to have a child!
The Chinese on your borders,
A son will slaughter them for you;
Upon the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
A servant will wreak havoc.
Your sorrow, if you have it, you will cast away.
When you have a child, my little foal,
You will name him Manas.
He will be a fierce gray-maned hero,
Commanding the whole world,
He will be a merciless lion.
His close companions will number eighty-four;
Wherever he strikes will be red fire.
No mortal will dare face him.
One whose face no enemy can bear to see,
Such a warrior you will have.
When you have a child, rich Jakyp,
His enemy in combat will be Kakanchyn,
His rival in battle will be Bakburchun.
His taking the fanged beasts means,
If he is born alive and well,
He will land upright on his soles;
The enemy who clashes with him will fall face down.
When you have a son, my Jakyp,
His spear will reach the whole world;
To our small people will come
The benefit of that child of yours.
A lion will be born to be our fortress,
An unshakable warrior will be born.
And finding a sword in your dream:
One who hews stone into a road,
Who breaks many and makes them a people,
Who pours blood into clear water,
Who makes the little river run with fat,
Whoever stirs his wrath,
He seizes and kills;
Named Manas, a lion among lions,
Ah, Jakyp, my little foal,
Such a son you are going to have!
If you grasped the moon and sun,
Your child will be called a hero.
My hero Jakyp, hear me:
Of the eighteen thousand worlds,
You will grasp the guiding handle!
If you strike with care, throughout the world
Your name will become known.
When you have a child, across the world
Your proclamation will spread!
When you have a child, my Jakyp,
That child will become a warrior,
All twelve parts of his body sound,
Beginning strife in the world,
He will perform memorable deeds.
The poor forty Kyrgyz households,
From the hands of the Black Kalmyks,
He will set them free!
Your taking the moon and sun means,
Into the Muslims' land
You drive the infidels,
